articles.title: Political Connections Shield Illicit Coffee Traders In Ethiopia, Study Alleges - The Reporter Ethiopia
articles.summary: Political Connections Shield Illicit Coffee Traders In Ethiopia, Study Alleges  The Reporter Ethiopia
articles.full_text:
A new study of southwest Ethiopia’s coffee sector alleges that politically connected traders benefit from selective law enforcement, fragmented regulation, and weak accountability, allowing illicit shipments to evade sanctions while smallholder farmers face mounting economic and land pressures.
The report, published by the Rift Valley Institute (RVI) as part of the Ethiopia Peace Research Facility’s Knowledge for Peace series, examines the political economy of production and trade across the Kaffa, Bench-Sheko, and Sheka zones of the Southwest Ethiopia Peoples’ Region. Written by Dubale Gebeyehu Genbezo and drawing on 47 in-depth interviews, the study argues that corruption and informal power networks have become deeply embedded in sector governance, influencing land allocation, licensing, trade enforcement, and export market access.
“Corruption in the context of the Kaffa–Bench-Sheko–Sheka belt is on another dimension. That is, it functions as a mode of governance, not an aberration,” the study states.
The research describes a system in which some regional and lower-level government officials straddle the line between regulating the trade and personally benefiting from private investments in it. Anonymous sources further alleged that politically connected actors have leveraged judicial and security institutions to retrieve confiscated illegal coffee shipments and shield traders from legal penalties.
These findings emerge as Ethiopia’s coffee industry continues to serve as a critical economic engine, generating 3 billion U.S. dollars in export earnings during the 2025/26 fiscal year. Meanwhile, the U.S. Department of Agriculture forecasts national production at 12.10 million 60-kilogram bags for the current marketing year. However, the report cautions that entrenched corruption and fragmented institutional frameworks threaten to undermine these gains and distort who benefits from the sector’s returns.
A central weakness identified in the study is the overlapping responsibilities among federal, regional, zonal, and district authorities. Institutions handling coffee policy, quality inspection, taxation, transportation, and security operate with intersecting mandates and little coordination. This structural ambiguity increases transaction costs for producers and cooperatives while giving politically connected actors room to negotiate preferential treatment.
“Rather than forming a coherent hierarchy, these entities often function as semiautonomous centres of authority with overlapping mandates and competing priorities. The absence of a single, authoritative coordinating institution produces structural ambiguity, with successive governments maximizing surplus extraction through trade regulation rather than institutional streamlining,” the report warns.
The research also scrutinizes a regional task force established to combat illicit trading. While intended to curb smuggling, the task force has allegedly contributed to the expansion of black-market channels through selective enforcement, uneven sanctions, and informal negotiations.
“In this context, illicit trade does not exist outside the state. Rather, it is mediated through fragmented and politicized state institutions,” the authors note, adding that frequent regulatory changes further erode trust in official rules.
The shift toward direct coffee sourcing has similarly altered power dynamics. Vertical integration—introduced to improve market access by allowing eligible exporters to bypass the Ethiopian Commodity Exchange (ECX)—has instead disadvantaged some cooperative unions while opening pathways for market concentration and regulatory arbitrage.
Furthermore, agricultural land allocation is a prominent source of conflict. Interviews with farmers, local administrators, and civil society representatives highlighted cases where investment licenses facilitated the displacement of communities from ancestral lands without adequate consultation, due process, or fair compensation. The report notes that forested landscapes used for shade-grown coffee receive little direct financial support or ecosystem compensation for local communities, even as agricultural expansion elsewhere enjoys fiscal backing. Vulnerable groups, including the Manjja and Majang communities as well as women farmers, face acute barriers to land ownership, cooperative participation, and agricultural services.
The study questions whether cooperative structures and ethical-trade certification schemes consistently deliver intended benefits. Certification premiums meant to support community development are reportedly captured in some cases by cooperative leaders or intermediaries, mirroring supply-chain inequalities. Smallholders, constrained by limited access to formal credit, often rely on advance payments or loans from traders; when harvests or prices fall short, farmers risk losing control of their land or becoming trapped in restrictive repayment terms.
Finally, the report warns that upcoming international mandates, such as the European Union’s Deforestation Regulation, could impose severe cost burdens on smallholders who must trace coffee back to specific production plots using geolocation data. Without public investment in traceability infrastructure and technical assistance, smallholders and forest-conserving cooperatives risk being priced out of key European markets.
To mitigate these risks, the study recommends establishing a statutory regional coffee governance council to clarify institutional responsibilities and fast-tracking the long-delayed opening of the National Coffee Museum in Bonga as a hub for research and community benefit.

articles.title: Engineering Ghana’s automotive and transport transformation: From import dependence to industrial growth - MyJoyOnline
articles.summary: Engineering Ghana’s automotive and transport transformation: From import dependence to industrial growth  MyJoyOnline
articles.full_text:
Audio By Carbonatix
Ghana’s automotive and transport sectors hold enormous potential for industrialisation, job creation, investment and economic growth. Realising this potential requires a shift from dependence on imported vehicles and reactive transport management towards local engineering, evidence-based planning, manufacturing and effective regulation.
My recommendations focus on five critical areas:
1. Local Manufacturing & Automotive Engineering
Ghana must move beyond vehicle assembly to vehicle design, component manufacturing, testing and production. We should connect universities, technical universities, Ghanaian engineers and local businesses with established international manufacturers to design and prototype vehicles suited to Ghanaian conditions—from affordable utility vehicles to agricultural and commercial transport. International partnerships should deliver manufacturing technology, quality assurance and skills transfer, while government incentives reward local content, employment and technology development. Successful products can serve Ghana and expand into African markets through the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
2. Stronger Institutions & Safer Vehicle Imports
Institutions such as the Ghana Automotive Development Centre must have the funding, skilled personnel and technical capacity to develop and implement internationally aligned policies. Applicable vehicle import and safety standards must be consistently enforced. Vehicles that fail the relevant requirements should be rejected or otherwise handled through lawful procedures. Consumer protection, roadworthiness and public safety must take priority.
3. Quality Assurance In The Spare-Parts Market
Ghana needs stronger verification and traceability of spare parts, particularly safety-critical components such as brakes, steering and suspension. Dealers should be supported in building relationships with reputable OEMs and legitimate aftermarket suppliers. Using DVLA registration data alongside vehicle age, component compatibility, failure rates and market demand would help guide imports towards parts needed by the active vehicle fleet. This can reduce unsuitable stock, improve availability and protect consumers from counterfeit or defective components, while assessing used parts according to their actual condition and safety.
4. Data-Driven Mobility & Congestion Reduction
We cannot effectively manage congestion without understanding passenger movements. Ghana needs reliable data on travel origins and destinations, passenger numbers, vehicle occupancy, routes, traffic volumes and journey times across different days and hours. For example, analysing travel between Kasoa and central Accra could help determine the right public transport capacity, routes and service frequency. Traffic surveys, GPS fleet data and responsibly managed digital information can guide planning, while Ghanaian technology companies develop useful commuter applications. Engineering studies should inform dedicated bus lanes, improved interchanges, coordinated traffic signals and better pedestrian facilities—avoiding both inadequate services and unnecessary oversupply.
5. Road Infrastructure & Safety As Engineering Priorities
Ghana recorded 2,949 road deaths, 14,743 crashes and 16,714 injuries in 2025, with fatalities increasing by 18.2% compared with 2024. We need coordinated action through safer road and junction design, effective enforcement, vehicle inspections, preventive fleet maintenance, proper drainage, visible road markings, pedestrian protection and reliable emergency response.
High-risk locations must be identified and interventions prioritised using crash data and measurable safety benefits. While major infrastructure programmes such as the Big Push are important, urban roads, traffic management and integrated public transport must also receive sustained attention. Short-term local initiatives cannot replace long-term planning of Ghana’s road networks and mobility systems.
The Way Forward
Ghana needs a coordinated national approach that brings together automotive manufacturing, engineering education, institutional reform, vehicle and spare-parts standards, transport data and safer infrastructure. These are connected challenges requiring practical, measurable solutions—not isolated interventions.
Our ambition must be greater than importing vehicles or easing traffic. It must be to build Ghanaian engineering capability, create local industrial value, reduce congestion, save lives, and establish Ghana as a competitive automotive and transport hub for Africa.
*************
Ing. Sadik Koli Abdul Rahim
Graduate Role Engineer Finalist — BMW & Rolls-Royce, UK
Autonomous Driving Project Engineer — Google Maps, UK
